purpose: Add a retained negative-control fixture that proves zizmor's excessive-permissions audit actually fires against real over-broad workflow permissions, rather than relying only on configuration and source review (docs/catalog-provenance.md lines 20-24; automation.json line 254). FIX ROUND CORRECTION (2026-09-23): the original receipt generalized from a single-job fixture (whose one job declares its own permissions block) that zizmor's excessive-permissions audit is pedantic-only and that the repository's regular-persona CI 'would not itself catch a real excessive-permissions regression'. This revision adds a second, multi-job fixture (no job declares its own permissions) and shows excessive-permissions DOES fire under --persona regular for that shape, narrowing the claim to the specific fixture shape it was actually tested on. This is a corrected/extended procedure, run once with a new preregistration below; the original single-job result was not re-run or altered.
preregistered: If zizmor run offline against a fixture declaring `permissions: write-all` plus a needless job-level `contents: write` produces a finding with ident excessive-permissions and High severity, that settles gap 0 in the supports_incumbent direction (the analyzer genuinely detects over-broad permissions, not just template-injection/unpinned-uses as the existing retained receipts show). If no such finding appears, or the fixture is rejected/errors, that refutes readiness and would change the verdict the other way. A secondary check preregistered before running: the excessive-permissions audit is gated behind --persona pedantic (not the --persona regular used by every other zizmor test in this repository), so a control run at --persona regular against the same fixture is expected to NOT show excessive-permissions; if it did show it under regular persona, that would mean the existing regular-persona test suite was already implicitly covering this and the gap would already have been closed by prior evidence, which is not the case per gap text.

result: New fixture blueprints/gap-wave2-20260923/zizmor-negative-control/negative-control.yml.txt declares workflow-level `permissions: write-all` and a needless job-level `contents: write` on its single job. Running zizmor offline at --persona pedantic against this fixture produces an excessive-permissions finding (confidence High, severity High, annotation 'uses write-all permissions', feature 'permissions: write-all') with exit code 13. The new test tests/test_zizmor_negative_control.py asserts this finding's ident, severity and annotation content, and additionally asserts that the same fixture under --persona regular produces zero excessive-permissions findings. All 3 new tests pass. FIX ROUND CORRECTION: the original receipt generalized this single fixture's pedantic-only downgrade into a general claim that excessive-permissions is a pedantic-only audit and that 'the repository's regular-persona CI scan would not itself catch a real excessive-permissions regression'. A second fixture (blueprints/gap-wave2-20260923/zizmor-negative-control/multi-job-no-job-permissions.yml.txt: same workflow-level `permissions: write-all`, two jobs, neither declaring its own job-level permissions block) was built and run under --persona regular; excessive-permissions DID fire for this shape (confidence High, severity High, same annotation, exit code 14). So the pedantic-only downgrade is a property of the original fixture's specific shape (a single job that declares its own permissions block appears to suppress or downgrade the workflow-level finding under regular persona), not a general property of the excessive-permissions audit. The generalized claim about the repository's regular-persona CI is retracted; whether it would catch a real excessive-permissions regression depends on the shape of the affected workflow (specifically, whether every job in it declares its own permissions block), which was not separately audited across .github/workflows here.

verdict_impact.explanation: Directly demonstrates zizmor's excessive-permissions audit fires on genuinely over-broad permissions with real, retained, re-runnable native execution across two fixture shapes, closing the gap between the scoped-permissions claim (previously configuration/source-review only) and actual analyzer behavior. The persona-gating behavior is more nuanced than originally reported: excessive-permissions fires under --persona regular for a multi-job fixture where no job declares its own permissions, and is downgraded to --persona pedantic only when a job in the fixture declares its own (narrower) permissions block, which likely reads as the workflow author having already scoped that job explicitly. This means the repository's regular-persona CI zizmor scan (validate.yml) would in fact catch an excessive-permissions regression in most real multi-job workflows, unless every affected job also declares its own permissions block.

limitations: The persona-downgrade mechanism was probed with exactly two fixture shapes (single job declaring its own permissions vs. two jobs where neither declares permissions); zizmor's actual internal rule for when excessive-permissions is downgraded to pedantic was not read from source, only inferred from these two observed behaviors, so edge cases (e.g. a multi-job workflow where only one of several jobs declares permissions) remain untested.

Only one over-permission pattern (write-all plus a needless job-level contents: write, and separately write-all with no job-level permissions) was tested; zizmor's excessive-permissions audit may have other trigger conditions (e.g. specific named scopes like `packages: write` without use) not exercised here.

This does not audit whether any of the repository's actual .github/workflows/*.yml files have the fixture-1 shape (workflow-level over-broad permissions plus every job declaring its own permissions) that would still only be caught under pedantic persona; that would require a separate pass over the real workflow files, out of scope for this check.
